newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Shekel weakens in roller-coaster trading.
newsitem.headline: Shekel weakens in roller-coaster trading.

text.p: The shekel representative rate was fixed slightly lower against the dollar on Wednesday in very volatile trading following a cabinet decision to widen the Israeli currency's trading band, dealers said.

After the government approved foreign currency reforms, a move that triggered the resignation of Finance Minister Dan Meridor, the Bank of Israel lowered its key lending rate by 1.2 percentage points to an annual 12.7 percent.
It was the first rate cut since February.

"During early trading the shekel weakened sharply as the market awaited the rate decision. The dollar was traded in a wide spread of about 3.4200/4800 as the rumour was that the Bank of Israel would lower its key lending rate by three percentage points," said Ilan Zadka at United Mizrahi Bank.
Zadka said that after the rate announcement the shekel recovered.
Meridor strongly opposed widening the shekel's trading bands, fearing it would lead to a further appreciation of the Israeli currency, hurt exports and cause the economy to slow.
"Trading was very volatile today and investors were confused. Volume was relatively low as investors remained on the sidelines trying to figure out what was going on," said Guy Levi at Bank Leumi.
Levi said the market was looking for direction.
"There are still some missing pieces as for instance who is going to be the next finance minister," he said. Meridor's resignation goes into effect on Friday.
The shekel had been allowed to trade in a band of seven percent above or below a diagonal slope designed to devalue it by six percent a year.
But high interest rates have buoyed the shekel, forcing the Bank of Israel to buy massive amounts of dollars to prevent the shekel from strengthening beyond its band.
Under the new plan the lower band remains the same while the upper band rises to 21 percent. The spread between the top and bottom band, therefore, will be 28 percent.
The central bank hopes it will no longer need to intervene constantly in the currency market.
But Zadka said he believed that the Bank of Israel would have to intervene again in trading on Thursday as the shekel might appreciate beyond its trading band.

"People do not realize that from an economic point of view Meridor is the main winner. The Bank of Israel had to cut the (interest) rate, and the lower diagonal limit remained unchanged, which will force the central bank to continue to buy dollars if the shekel rises," he said.

The representative rate for the dollar was fixed at 3.4200 shekels, against 3.4170 on Tuesday. The basket, composed of the dollar, mark, pound sterling, French franc and yen, was fixed at 3.7155 against 3.7074 on Tuesday.
On the crosses, the shekel traded against the yen at 3.0191 shekels per 100 yen compared with 3.0051 on Tuesday, and against the mark at 1.9802 shekels compared with 1.9684 on Tuesday.
- Dan Gerstenfeld, Tel Aviv newsroom, 972-3-537-2211 x233
